claims.text: The Deepwater Horizon explosion killed 11 workers and released millions of barrels of oil into the Gulf of Mexico
Hayward's 'I'd like my life back' comment during congressional testimony became a symbol of his perceived insensitivity
The BP board asked Hayward to step down and named Robert Dudley as his successor
Robert Dudley officially assumed the CEO role on October 1, 2010
BP agreed to pay $4.5 billion in criminal penalties in 2011, with additional civil settlements bringing total costs above $65 billion

outcome.summary: Hayward resigned as BP CEO in July 2010 and was succeeded by Robert Dudley. BP faced extensive criminal and civil penalties, ultimately paying over $65 billion in fines, settlements, and cleanup costs. The company's reputation was severely damaged and it sold off assets to cover liabilities.

timeline.event: Deepwater Horizon drilling rig explodes in the Gulf of Mexico, killing 11 workers
Hayward testifies before US Congress and says 'I'd like my life back'
BP board announces Hayward will step down as CEO, replaced by Robert Dudley
Robert Dudley officially takes over as BP CEO
BP agrees to a record $4.5 billion criminal penalty for the disaster

title: Tony Hayward resigns as BP CEO after Deepwater Horizon
trigger: The Deepwater Horizon oil spill in April 2010 became the largest marine oil spill in history, and Hayward's perceived mishandling of the crisis—including his remark 'I'd like my life back'—led the BP board to ask for his resignation.
